clue.text: At the end of the day, a lovable rogue

definitions.text: At the end of the day

parts.note: the article, kept as it is

indicators.note: a rogue letter strays out of line, so LOVABLE's letters are scattered

explanation.surface: Someone sums up a charming scoundrel: when all is said and done, he is a lovable rogue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lovable rogue' is a stock phrase, so 'rogue' hides as a noun when it is really the adjective scrambling LOVABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: 'At the end of the day' and 'above all' are both ways of saying 'most importantly, in the final reckoning'.

clue.text: Flatness of a route's variable

parts.note: the article, kept as it is
algebra's variables are x, y and z

explanation.surface: A cyclist or surveyor asks how level a stretch of road is along its changing course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flatness' reads as a physical property of a road; here it is the emotional kind. The 's stands for 'has', joining PATH to Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Apathy is emotional flatness, a lack of feeling or enthusiasm.

clue.text: Old boy, solitary and square, extremely chaste date

parts.note: OB = old boy, a former pupil
S = square, as in maps and abbreviations

indicators.note: the extremes of CHASTE are its outer letters

explanation.surface: A lonely, old-fashioned former schoolboy goes on a very proper date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Date' looks like a romantic outing for the chaste old boy; it is the verb, to become dated.
explanation.definitionFit: To obsolesce is to become obsolete, which is what 'date' means as an intransitive verb.

clue.text: Folly to have run into deserted cape

parts.note: to have headed somewhere is to have run or made for it
a ness is a headland or cape, as in Orford Ness or Buchan Ness

explanation.surface: Someone foolishly runs off to an abandoned headland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deserted cape' reads as a lonely headland, but it is two words, and 'to have run' goes between them. A ness is a headland in British place names.
explanation.definitionFit: Empty-headedness, having nothing in one's head, is folly or silliness.

clue.text: The French bay is severely run down

parts.note: to bay is to howl or shout

explanation.surface: A French bay has become badly neglected and shabby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bay' looks like a stretch of coast after 'The French'; it is the hound's cry. 'Run down' is not shabby but 'criticise'.
explanation.definitionFit: To lash out is to attack verbally with force, i.e. to run someone down severely.

clue.text: German army unit

explanation.surface: A regiment or division of the German military.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as 'army unit'; in fact 'unit' stands alone as the definition, and 'army' only gives FORCE.
explanation.definitionFit: A g-force is a unit of acceleration equal to the pull of Earth's gravity.

clue.text: Tricky to anticipate surplus of rifles in mess

indicators.note: a mess is a jumble, so the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: Soldiers find it hard to predict how many spare rifles will turn up in the mess hall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mess' wants to be the soldiers' dining room, which fits the rifles; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something full of surprises keeps doing what you did not expect, so it is tricky to anticipate.

clue.text: In her novel, there's a valley

definitions.note: the Rhine is the river; the clue leans on the Rhine valley

indicators.note: novel means new, so IN HER is made into something new

explanation.surface: A reader notes that a valley features in some woman's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' reads as the book in which the valley appears; it is the adjective 'new', rearranging IN HER.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhine gives its name to a famous valley; the definition is loose, which is why it sits vaguely at the end.

clue.text: Breeze drifts over Tyneside, making someone cold

indicators.note: letters that drift wander out of their order

parts.note: Tyneside, round Newcastle, is in the North East (NE) of England

explanation.surface: A wind blowing across Newcastle leaves someone shivering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Someone cold' is not a chilly Geordie but a cold-hearted man: Ebenezer Scrooge of Dickens's A Christmas Carol.
explanation.definitionFit: Ebenezer Scrooge is literature's byword for a cold, unfeeling miser.

clue.text: Even the old hippies do this

parts.note: ye is an old form of 'the', as in 'Ye Olde Tea Shoppe'

explanation.surface: A remark that even aging hippies still do something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Even' reads as the adverb 'even the old ones'; it is the adjective 'level', giving TIED.
explanation.definitionFit: Tie-dyeing T-shirts in swirls of colour is the classic hippie craft of the 1960s.

clue.text: Strike a pose, fabulous figure?

indicators.note: to strike a pose is to rearrange oneself, and here A POSE's letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A photographer tells a model with a gorgeous body to strike a pose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fabulous figure' suggests a great body; 'fabulous' is literal here: a figure famous for fables.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop is the ancient Greek teller of fables, so literally a fabulous figure.

clue.text: Composition of quiet soul

parts.note: the soul is one's life force, as in 'the life and soul of the party'

explanation.surface: A reflective piece of music written by a quiet, gentle person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composition' reads as music; it is a painting's arrangement of objects.
explanation.definitionFit: A still life is a painted composition of inanimate objects such as fruit and flowers.

clue.text: 50 admitted to pious golf club in California suburb

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for 50
a wood is a type of golf club

explanation.surface: Fifty new members join a devout golf club somewhere in California.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Golf club' reads as a members' club that admits the fifty; it is just the stick, WOOD.
explanation.definitionFit: Hollywood is a district of Los Angeles, California.

clue.text: Enormous honour's meeting earl

parts.note: OBE (Order of the British Empire), a British honour, plus the S of 's

explanation.surface: A tremendous honour: getting to meet an earl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enormous' reads as praise for the honour; it is the plain adjective 'very fat'. The OBE is a British honour given by the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Obese means extremely fat, i.e. enormous in size.

clue.text: Face of donkey kissed noisily

indicators.note: done noisily means said out loud, so we go by sound

parts.note: ass = donkey, pecked = kissed (a quick peck)

explanation.surface: A donkey's face gets a loud, smacking kiss.
explanation.walkthrough: A peck is a quick kiss, so 'kissed' is PECKED.
explanation.definitionFit: An aspect is a face or side of something, as in one face of a problem.

clue.text: Vociferously against taking pudding through to bedroom

indicators.note: vociferously means loudly spoken, so we go by sound

parts.note: on = against (leaning on a wall), taking the sweet (pudding)

explanation.surface: Someone loudly objects to having dessert carried up to the bedroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Against' reads as opposition; it is ON in the sense of leaning against. Pudding and sweet are British words for dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: An en-suite bathroom opens directly off a bedroom, so it is reached through to the bedroom.

clue.text: Composed of sane mind, I will be a mole

indicators.note: the answer is composed, put together, from the letters that follow

explanation.surface: A double agent reassures himself that with a calm head he will make a good spy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composed' tempts you to read calm, which suits 'sane mind'; it means assembled.
explanation.definitionFit: A mole is a spy planted within an organisation, an inside man.

clue.text: Once snared by lasso on a sierra

indicators.note: the answer is caught inside the words that follow, like an animal in a snare

explanation.surface: A creature caught once with a lasso on a mountain range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' looks like 'formerly'; it is the conjunction, as in 'once you arrive'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Once you arrive' and 'as soon as you arrive' mean the same.

clue.text: Waster, poet, communist

definitions.meaning: someone who wastes money, a squanderer
Stephen, English poet of Auden's 1930s circle
the same poet briefly joined the Communist Party in the 1930s

explanation.walkthrough: Three definitions: a spender wastes money; Stephen Spender was an English poet; and he briefly joined the Communist Party in the 1930s.
explanation.definitionFit: A spender uses up money; Spender the poet was also, for a time, a communist.

clue.text: Parrot in old TV show

definitions.meaning: the verb: to say back words mechanically
a programme shown again after its first broadcast

explanation.surface: A parrot appears in a television show from the past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parrot' is the verb, to say again what one hears.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the verb is a plain synonym of parroting, and the noun is the broadcasters' word for a rerun.

clue.text: Is concerned about son, gives show of affection

explanation.surface: A worried parent hugs their son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gives' reads as part of the definition's verb phrase; it only joins the wordplay to the noun 'show of affection'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a gentle, loving stroke of the hand is the physical form the affection takes.

clue.text: Train company greet stranger

indicators.note: made stranger, GREET becomes odder in shape

explanation.surface: A rail firm's staff welcome an unfamiliar passenger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train company' reads as a railway operator, and 'stranger' as a noun; 'Train' is a procession and 'stranger' is 'more odd'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cortege is a procession or train of attendants, especially at a funeral.

clue.text: City's bankrupt financiers, hard to ignore

parts.note: Lehman Brothers, the investment bank whose bankruptcy in 2008 set off the financial crisis

explanation.surface: The City of London's failed bankers are too hard to ignore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City' looks like the City of London, the financial district that fits the financiers; it is a French city.
explanation.definitionFit: Le Mans is a city in north-west France, famous for its 24-hour motor race.

clue.text: Had put robe on (not grand)

parts.note: to be gowned is to have put on a robe

explanation.surface: Someone had dressed in a robe, though not a grand one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had' looks like an auxiliary verb for 'put'; it is the definition, meaning possessed.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the possessive sense of 'had', as in 'had a car'.

clue.text: Celebrated being ruggedly toned

indicators.note: rugged means rough and broken, so TONED is roughed up

explanation.surface: A film star is admired for their rugged, muscular physique.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Celebrated' reads as a past tense verb, 'was celebrated'; it is the adjective 'famous'.
explanation.definitionFit: Noted and celebrated both mean famous.

clue.text: Bigot at heart, host's without skill, dignity?

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside
the heart of BIGOT is its middle letter

explanation.surface: A bigoted TV presenter, lacking talent, still demands respect.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Partridge is Steve Coogan's comic creation, a gauche, self-important British TV and radio host; hence the question mark. 'Without' is the old sense 'outside', so dignity wraps around the other two.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Partridge is a fictional chat-show host, so 'host' defines him by example.

clue.text: Wasting time in Tate Modern, busy tourist spot

indicators.note: busy letters bustle about and end up in a new order

parts.note: T = time, removed from the fodder
anagram fodder once one T is gone

explanation.surface: A complaint about queues wasting time at a crowded London gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: Tate Modern is a London art gallery, and beside 'busy tourist spot' it looks like the answer; it is the fodder, and 'busy' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Notre-Dame cathedral in Paris is one of the most visited sights in Europe.

clue.text: Early on, state administered by old New Zealander?

definitions.text: Early on, state administered by old New Zealander?

indicators.note: early on in each word means its first letter

parts.note: the first letters of State Administered
the moa is an extinct giant flightless bird of New Zealand

explanation.surface: A history note about a young nation governed in its early days by a New Zealand elder.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the old New Zealander is an extinct bird, not a colonial officer, yet Western Samoa was run by New Zealand from 1914 until independence in 1962, and the question mark flags the double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: Samoa was, early in the last century, a state administered by New Zealand.

clue.text: 'Savage'!? Sorry, it's 'unruly'

indicators.note: unruly letters will not stay in line

explanation.surface: Someone corrects a word: not savage, sorry, the right word is unruly.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make it look like an editor swapping one word for another; 'Savage' is a noun, and 'Sorry' is SAD rather than an apology.
explanation.definitionFit: A sadist, who enjoys inflicting pain, is a savage, a cruel person.

clue.text: What toffs shoot, short-of-height bumpkins

parts.note: pheasant shooting is a traditional sport of the British upper classes; a toff is a posh person

explanation.surface: Posh hunters take aim at short country folk.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sets toffs against bumpkins, class against class; the bumpkins are the definition and the toffs' quarry supplies the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Peasants, rustic country people, are bumpkins.
